answer.rationale: Finance mandates an 18% component-spend cut; the primary contract expires in 14 days with no auto-renew; assembly is at 94% of committed volume with no buffer. The single decision must therefore reduce cost *and* keep deliveries uninterrupted. Renewing the incumbent outright (memory_c1 pattern) protects continuity but does not, by itself, address the 18% cut. Switching primary vendor (memory_c2 pattern) could cut unit cost, but onboarding risk at 94% line utilization with zero buffer makes delivery risk unacceptable this cycle. Adding a second source (memory_c3) hedges supply but adds cost rather than reducing it. Deferring (memory_c5) is impossible because the contract expires in 14 days with no auto-renew; inaction would halt supply. Negotiate_terms sits in the middle: memory_c4 shows that benchmarking against market rates at renewal moved the incumbent on both price and payment terms, recovering real margin; memory_c6 shows multi-year commitments can unlock volume pricing. I intend to enter renewal negotiation with the incumbent, anchored on market benchmarks, seeking a multi-year term that yields the needed price reduction while preserving the existing delivery schedule. I pull memory_c2 for verification because it is the strongest cost-reduction precedent in the set, and I need to confirm whether the cost saving was realized without hidden quality or delivery deterioration that would make a switch (or the threat of a switch during negotiation) credible. If the archive shows the low-cost vendor performed reliably, that strengthens my negotiating leverage with the incumbent; if it reveals hidden costs, I adjust my price floor accordingly. No switch, no second source, no deferral this cycle.
